question: Describe a situation where unexpected external factors forced major changes to your plans.

raiseTranscript.text: Describe a situation where unexpected external factors forced major changes to your plans.

Our team was building a feature for a new API partner. Two weeks before launch the partner changed their auth requirements. I had to rewrite the integration layer in five days while still hitting the original date.
How did you handle the rewrite and what did you learn?

I broke the work into daily check-ins with my mentor, flagged two scope cuts, and shipped a minimal version that still passed their new tests. The biggest lesson was asking for help earlier instead of trying to absorb everything alone.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a situation where unexpected external factors forced major changes to your plans.
Role: new grad on small feature team
Situation: partner changed auth specs 2 weeks out
Actions: daily mentor syncs, proposed scope cuts, shipped minimal viable integration
Outcome: met launch date with reduced scope
Quote: "I should have asked for help earlier instead of trying to absorb everything alone."
Follow-up: Asked how they decided what to cut; candidate described clear trade-off list they brought to mentor.
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Adaptability at junior level. The candidate owned an individual deliverable that was derailed by an external partner change and responded by creating daily visibility with a mentor and making explicit scope trade-offs. The quote about asking for help earlier shows coachability and learning from the event. Scope stayed within one feature and one teammate, which matches expectations for 0-2 years. The main gap is lack of evidence that the candidate surfaced the change to anyone outside their immediate mentor.

What did you do differently after that?
I just worked harder the next time and hoped nothing else would change.

At junior level we look for evidence that the person can absorb feedback and adapt their own execution; neither is present here.

raiseTranscript.text: Describe a situation where unexpected external factors forced major changes to your plans.
A key upstream service we depended on was deprecated with 30 days notice. I coordinated with three other teams to shift to the new service while keeping our quarterly OKR intact.
I ran a two-day spike across teams, published a one-page decision doc with latency and cost options, and got the directors to agree on a phased migration that protected our launch date.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a situation where unexpected external factors forced major changes to your plans.
Role: senior IC owning cross-team dependency
Situation: upstream service deprecated with 30-day notice
Actions: organized multi-team spike, wrote decision doc, drove phased migration plan
Outcome: protected quarterly OKR and aligned three directors
Quote: "I ran a two-day spike across teams and published a one-page decision doc."
Follow-up: How they influenced without authority; candidate described using data and a written doc rather than escalation.
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Adaptability at senior level. The candidate turned an external deprecation into a coordinated cross-team migration while protecting an OKR. They used a written decision document and a short spike to create alignment without authority, which is the expected influence pattern. Scope involved multiple teams and a visible deliverable, fitting 3-7 years experience. The only missing element is a quantified impact on the broader org beyond the immediate OKR.

raiseTranscript.text: Describe a situation where unexpected external factors forced major changes to your plans.
Regulatory changes in two markets required us to pause a major product rollout. I reallocated two teams to compliance work and reset expectations with the exec team.
How did you handle the team impact?
I met with each manager, protected their highest performers from context switching, and created a six-week recovery plan that still let the teams hit their career goals.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a situation where unexpected external factors forced major changes to your plans.
Role: manager of two teams
Situation: regulatory change paused product rollout
Actions: reallocated teams, reset exec expectations, protected career goals in recovery plan
Outcome: compliance work completed without losing key talent
Quote: "I protected their highest performers from context switching and created a six-week recovery plan."
Follow-up: How they decided which work to pause; candidate described explicit prioritization with the directors.
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Adaptability at manager level. The candidate absorbed a regulatory shock by reallocating team capacity and resetting stakeholder expectations while protecting individual career plans. This shows both team-level leverage and people development under pressure. The story stays at the team and director level, which is appropriate for a manager. The gap is limited visibility into longer-term org process changes that might prevent similar shocks.

raiseTranscript.text: Describe a situation where unexpected external factors forced major changes to your plans.

A sudden tariff change increased our hardware costs by 18 percent and threatened the entire P&L for the year. I led a six-week strategic review that shifted us to a new supplier region and renegotiated two major contracts.
We reduced supply-chain concentration risk and created a board-approved three-year sourcing strategy that the CFO now uses as the model for other product lines.

Outcome: lowered concentration risk and created reusable board model
Quote: "We reduced supply-chain concentration risk and created a board-approved three-year sourcing strategy."

exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Adaptability at exec level. Scope spans P&L, contracts, and multi-year planning, which matches 10+ year expectations. The story demonstrates strategic judgment and organizational leverage rather than heroics. The only minor gap is lack of detail on how the change was socialized with the broader leadership team before the board review.
